In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the prevalence of HIV infection in women of reproductive age in a given area is likely to be at least 1.2 times and probably more than 1.5 times that estimated from serosurveys of pregnant women in that area.
HIV prevalence among pregnant women is a biased estimate of prevalence in the general female population.

the prevalence ratio for HIV among pregnant women to all women in the same general population is likely to be 1.2 (range 1.0 to 2.0) in sub-Saharan Africa and 1.0 (range 0.7 to 1.4) in other parts of the world.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HIV prevalence ratio for pregnant women is not constant and is influenced by a number of factors.
the ratio of prevalence in the two groups can be used to adjust the HIV prevalence in pregnant women in order to estimate the HIV prevalence in the general female population.
, in the absence of a reliable denominator, HIV prevalence in pregnant women should not be used to estimate HIV prevalence in women of reproductive age.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HIV serosurveillance in pregnant women is not a reliable proxy for HIV prevalence in the general female population.
HIV prevalence estimates in pregnant women can be used to infer HIV prevalence in the female population, but the estimates should be interpreted in a culturally specific context.

HIV seroprevelance data from pregnant women can be used to make inferences about the prevalence of HIV among women of reproductive age, but that the inferences should be interpreted in light of the biases that may affect the relationship between the two populations.
